subtitulo: Economic miracle, emigration, the colonels and Cyprus: why the Greek army turned right and the Peruvian army turned left (1949–1974)

coda.heading: Resonances 2024–2026 and coda for the trip
intro: Cyprus remains divided and is, along with the Aegean disputes, the permanent knot of Greek-Turkish relations; the diplomatic thaw of 2023–2026 has left it deliberately off the agenda because it has no negotiated solution in sight. The commemoration of the Polytechnic every November 17 remains an annual political event, with a march on the American embassy and the usual disturbances, and 2023 marked its fiftieth anniversary. And the debate over state surveillance returned forcefully in Greece between 2022 and 2024 following the wiretapping scandal at the intelligence service and the use of spyware against journalists and politicians, which reactivated, with new technology, exactly the discussion from dispatch 20 about the apparatus that outlives regimes.

items.text: For the trip: in Athens, the Polytechnic gate on Patission Street, with its monument; and the avenue where it happened. In Exarchia, the adjoining neighborhood, you'll see street politics, graffiti and a symbolic density that is best read in the context of this dispatch and not as picturesque color. And look at the apartment blocks with the eye of antiparochí: they are the built record of how a country absorbed its internal migration.

In Corfu, the colonels' period was experienced at a relative remove, but it was also the start of mass tourism: the sixties and seventies transformed the island's economy more than any political event did. Ask about that — about when the first big hotel arrived, about what families did before. It is the doorway into Block V, which begins in 1974 and runs up to the month of your trip.

sections.heading: The miracle and its safety valve
paragraphs: Between 1950 and 1973, the Greek economy grew at rates only Japan surpassed anywhere in the world: around seven percent annually, sustained for two decades. The country partially industrialized, was electrified, built infrastructure with American aid from the Marshall Plan, and its standard of living was transformed.

That growth rested on three pillars worth naming, because they explain the fragility that followed. The first: the merchant marine, with the privileged tax regime we examined in dispatch 12. The second: tourism, which took off in the sixties. The third, and the least discussed: EMIGRATION. Between 1950 and 1974, hundreds of thousands of people left Greece — the 1960 recruitment agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany channeled most of them — reaching, by the broadest estimates, close to a million out of a population of eight. Their remittances were one of the country's principal sources of foreign currency.

Emigration functioned, as in twentieth-century Peru and as in every periphery, as a social safety valve: it exported unemployment, exported potential conflict, and imported money. And it produced a working-class diaspora — very different from the commercial bourgeoisie of dispatch 12 — whose children and grandchildren remain in Germany, Australia and the United States, and whose relationship to Greece is one of a second home, remittances and summer visits. When German media in 2010 spoke of lazy Greeks, they were speaking of a country whose labor force had built a good part of Germany's own postwar miracle.

sections.heading: How the Athens you're about to see was built
paragraphs: Pause on a material detail that will explain everything you see through the taxi window from the airport: the five- or six-story apartment blocks, with continuous balconies and awnings, that cover miles of city with barely any variation. They are called POLYKATOIKIA and are the result of a specific mechanism called ANTIPAROCHI.

The system worked like this: the owner of a low house with land would hand the land over to a small builder, who would construct the block at his own expense and hand back to the owner an agreed number of apartments, keeping the rest to sell. No bank credit was needed, no large real-estate capital, no state intervention. Between the fifties and the seventies, that barter built the whole of Athens and absorbed the massive internal migration from the countryside.

The sociological consequences are enormous, and they explain Greek traits that would otherwise be puzzling. First: homeownership spread extraordinarily — Greece has one of the highest homeownership rates in Europe — and with it a widely distributed small urban property that cushioned inequality and explains how thousands of families survived the 2010 crisis without paying rent. Second: no concentrated real-estate capital formed, nor a propertyless urban proletariat, which weakened classic class conflicts. Third: the city grew without planning, without sufficient green space and with brutal density, because every building was a private decision. Fourth: social mixing is high — in the same block, different strata can live side by side, floor by floor — something quite uncommon in Latin America.

Compare it with Lima, where internal migration produced self-built shantytowns on the periphery, with land invasions, slow formalization and marked spatial segregation. Two popular solutions to the same problem — housing millions of migrants without a housing policy — with very different urban and political results. Athens's solution produced homeowners integrated into the center; Lima's produced homeowners on the periphery. That difference shows today in the shape of the two cities and in the shape of their conflicts.

sections.heading: The parallel system and the coup of April 21
paragraphs: Postwar Greek democracy was a tutelary one. Above the elected government operated three powers that answered to no vote: the crown, the military high command — with the IDEA officers' lodge as its core — and the American embassy, whose intervention in domestic politics was open and acknowledged. The left was banned, and its electorate voted for a tolerated stand-in formation; the files kept functioning.

Two episodes show the system in action. In May 1963, the pacifist deputy Grigoris Lambrakis was assassinated in Salonica by thugs linked to the police, and the investigation uncovered a web of official complicity; the case inspired Vassilikos's novel and Costa-Gavras's film Z, which in 1969 would do more to make the Greek situation known to the world than any diplomatic campaign. In July 1965, King Constantine II forced the fall of Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou, elected with a broad majority, and bought off deputies to form alternative governments: the episode known as the Apostasia opened two years of crisis.

On April 21, 1967, weeks before elections the center would probably have won, a group of colonels seized power using a NATO plan drawn up for cases of Communist insurrection. The dictatorship lasted seven years. Its ideology was summed up in the slogan of a Greece of Greek Christians; its practice was prior censorship, dissolution of parties, deportation to islands, systematic torture in military police premises, and a cultural repression that went as far as banning Theodorakis's music, policing long hair and miniskirts, and censoring the classics all over again. The regime was recognized and sustained internationally within the framework of the Cold War.

On November 17, 1973, the student occupation of the Athens Polytechnic was crushed by a tank that broke down the gate; there were deaths both inside and outside the compound, and the date became modern Greece's most important civic anniversary. A week later, an internal coup brought to power Brigadier Ioannidis, head of the military police, with an even harder line.

sections.heading: Cyprus 1974: the dictatorship destroys itself
paragraphs: Ioannidis tried to resolve the Cyprus question by force. On July 15, 1974, the Cypriot National Guard, led by Greek officers, staged a coup against President Makarios to impose union with Greece. Five days later, Turkey invoked its status as a guarantor power and invaded the island; in August, a second offensive gave it control of roughly thirty-six percent of the territory.

The human consequences were massive: around one hundred sixty thousand Greek Cypriots displaced southward and several tens of thousands of Turkish Cypriots displaced northward, in another de facto population exchange — the third in this history, after 1923 and the displacements of the civil war. Nicosia remains, in 2026, Europe's last divided capital, with the Green Line patrolled by the United Nations for more than half a century, and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus recognized by no one but Turkey. Every round of negotiation has failed, including the Annan Plan rejected in a referendum by Greek Cypriots in 2004.

The colonels' regime collapsed on July 23, 1974, unable to sustain a war it had itself provoked. The military chiefs summoned Konstantinos Karamanlis, exiled in Paris, to take over the government. The Metapolitefsi begins — the subject of the next dispatch.

sections.heading: 1968: two armies, two directions
paragraphs: Here is the contrast I promised, and the one I find most instructive in the whole block.

In April 1967, the Greek army staged a far-right coup to block a reformist center from reaching power, with tacit U.S. backing and under a national-security doctrine. In October 1968, the Peruvian army staged a coup and installed a government that expropriated the International Petroleum Company within days, promulgated in 1969 the deepest agrarian reform in Latin America after Cuba's, nationalized strategic sectors, created a system of social property, recognized Quechua as an official language in 1975, and replaced Indian Day with Peasant Day. Both institutions were Latin American or European armed forces of the same era, formed in part in American schools, acting under the same global Cold War framework, and they moved in opposite directions.

The explanation lies not in ideas but in structural position. The Greek army was the victor of a civil war against communism, with an institutional identity built on that victory, integrated into NATO on the border of the Soviet bloc, and tied by social origin and clientele to the right and the crown. The Peruvian army was an institution whose officers increasingly came from provincial middle sectors, formed at CAEM in a doctrine that defined underdevelopment and the landowning oligarchy as the real threats to national security, and which had fought guerrillas in 1965 and concluded that the problem was the agrarian structure. Two military institutions bearing the same label and moving in inverse trajectories, because their relationship to the internal social structure was different.

The methodological conclusion holds for the whole plan: generic categories — the army, the Church, the bourgeoisie, the state — explain nothing by themselves. What explains is the concrete position of each institution within its own history of conflicts. That is why this comparative exercise between Greece and Peru works better when it finds differences than when it finds similarities.
The final coincidence is chronological: Greece recovers democracy in 1974, Peru in 1980. And here the trajectories diverge dramatically once again, as we will see in the next dispatch.
